Messages.Author: James Hamblin
Messages.Body:
Here's a situation that came up tonight; I just want to make sure that
my play would not be considered "illegal" under the new rules.

I playing a bleed deck which relies on +1 stealth actions getting
through (think Mind Numbs and Marijava Ghouls), and my prey was a light
intercept deck with plenty of permanent intercept and untaps. I was
down to 7 pool. My predator was playing a Hostile Takeover/Parity Shift
deck, and had just played a Hostile Takeover on one of my (two)
vampires. He bids 3, and has 7 pool. If I allow him to have my
vampire, he can call two Parity Shifts to kill me (5-player table), and
this seemed likely given the cards he had already played. If I bid
higher, I certainly would get bled out or voted out. My reason was to
simply oust myself (by bidding 14), so that my predator only got my VP
and 6 pool (which he was going to get anyway), and _not_ any more of my
vampires (which he could theoretically have used to help him sweep the
table).

Now, my only real justification here is "I don't want my predator to
sweep the table." Does that count as an out-of-game consideration?

James
--

| James Hamblin | Graduate Student, KTI Fellow |
| ham...@math.wisc.edu | University of Wisconsin -- Madison |

[clip]

> Now, my only real justification here is "I don't want my predator to
> sweep the table." Does that count as an out-of-game consideration?

I'm pretty sure I've seen LSJ post that a player in a lost position may choose
the manner of thier ousting. You could have helped your predator to sweep,
prevented him from sweeping, or done any other thing you please.

Rather than read "no out of game considerations" (or, as I prefer to say it, "no
out of game goals") as a seperate rule, read it as another way of saying "Play
toward the in-game goal of trying to win the current game and not toward any out
of game goals".

-Robert

I'm quite certain it will be made more clear.

> Personally, I think it's too convoluted and too open to subjective
> interpretations while at the same time *not* powerful enough to stop
> the abuses it aims at stopping.

The issues facing numerous tournaments were:
1) Ousting someone cross-table who you didn't want to face in the finals.
2) Ousting someone because of thier V:EKN rating.
3) Ousting someone to keep them from qualifying for an invitation only event.

I agree that it will not stop the abuses listed above. Some players, intent on
cheating, will create cover stories. It could take a while for the judge(s) to
catch on to their antics. Again, this is like the collusion rules and
deck-marking rules that we've always had. While far from perfectly detectable
and enforcable it *will* positively affect the environment and future events
will be closer to this ideal than the former events. This is true because:

1) Many players won't cheat because it is against the rules (even if they are
smart enough to get away with it). Many players openly pursued the goals listed
above because they thought it was OK to do so. Now that it is not OK, they will
stop.
2) The rule will catch players who are blatant or open in thier attempts to
pursue goals outside of the current game.

>The issues facing numerous tournaments were:
>1) Ousting someone cross-table who you didn't want to face in the finals.

Agree. While this could be construed as smart play, it sucks to be on
the receiving end, so I agree that this can be a problem.

>2) Ousting someone because of thier V:EKN rating.

Has this ever happened to anyone's knowledge? And BTW, is hitting
someone becasue they seem to be a threat to your win (because you know
them to have a high rating and be a great player) OK?

>3) Ousting someone to keep them from qualifying for an invitation only event.

Again, is this an actaul (rather than a theoretical) problem?

>I agree that it will not stop the abuses listed above. Some players, intent on
>cheating, will create cover stories. It could take a while for the judge(s) to
>catch on to their antics. Again, this is like the collusion rules and
>deck-marking rules that we've always had. While far from perfectly detectable
>and enforcable it *will* positively affect the environment and future events
>will be closer to this ideal than the former events. This is true because:
>
>1) Many players won't cheat because it is against the rules (even if they are
>smart enough to get away with it). Many players openly pursued the goals listed
>above because they thought it was OK to do so. Now that it is not OK, they will
>stop.

Agree. I really do.

However, it's not a good rule if it only stops morally upright people.
And what I think is the major problem is that the rules are not really
enforceable as long as the perpetrator has some amount of
intelligence.

>2) The rule will catch players who are blatant or open in thier attempts to
>pursue goals outside of the current game.

That is, it will force people to lie more and better... ;-)

I think a better way of doing it would be not to reward this kind of
behaviour, rather than trying to stop it. For instance, giving one (1)
"tournament winning point" to the winner, and the winner only [1],
would eliminate most of the problems without the extreme ambiguity and
subjectivity the current rules suffer under [2]. Yes, players that see
their position as totally hopeless could still profit from messing up
people cross-table, but it's probably not a major problem.

Also, the tournament points should be kept as secret as possible.

[1] Probably splitting this point among tied winners, although this
would open the way for bad dealings again.

[2] And would also make the 3-2 table split useless, which is a good
thing IMO.

a referee at all, because that would be worse for the game than
having a (human, fallible) referee.

I recommend sticking with human judges making human judgement
calls until we come up with a better, kinder, smarter, less
fallible sort of life form. Like Aibo.

gomi

Messages.Author: Jason Bell
Messages.Body:
"LSJ" <vte...@white-wolf.com> wrote

> Johan Lundstrom wrote:
> > Xian <xi...@NOSPAMwaste.org> wrote:
> > >Thus, the judge has to depend on the reported reasons, etc. It's a
> > >*judgement* call.
> >
> > Exactly. Surely that's problematic.
>
> If anyone has a reasonable suggestion for a way to run a V:TES tournament
> without a judge, I'm open to it.

You're missing the point. The idea is to avoid rules which, by their
nature, require judgement calls. The judge should know the rules,
and be able to accurately settle any rules dispute between two
players (such as, non-replacement of Bum's Rush if blocked, or the
timing on Propaganda).

The more responsibilities that judges must carry beyond
this primary function will make the judge's job much more difficult
and cause harm to a tournament.

Look at it this way. If a player knows the rules well, he should
have no fear of a judge coming to the table, as that player will
already know how the ruling will go. The more the judge is
empowered or required to make game-altering rulings based
upon his judgement, the edgier these situations will become.

Will the player be warned or even tossed if he doesn't kiss up to
the judge? Will the judge be more harsh if he hasn't had enough
sleep, or if he has been called to this table before? Will "known"
players be given more discretion on cross-table maneuvers
because their desire and ability to win is known and trusted?

These should not be questions a player has to consider
as a judge is summoned to the table.

- Jason Bell

Messages.Author: Matt Latham
Messages.Body:
Something important thats being glossed over here.

THIS IS ALL SO SAD.

VTES used to be a low-player count game that was known for valuing a
fun table dynamic and politics over Degeneracy and cheating.
"Collusion" was "politics", being a toadie was an accepted practice.

Magic had the Cheaters and Powergamers, Jyhad had the gamers and
socializers.

Now WW felt that they had to add collusion rules to VTES? Have we, the
playing masses, sunk so low as to require Magic rules in VTES? Has
winning the "big prize" become more important than playing the game?

I remember 36 people at Origins 1998 playing VTES, with practically no
prize support (I won it and got two starters of VTES and two boosters
of Sabbat as my prize), playing for the fun of the game.

I love the real prize support you all get now but if it came at the
cost of requiring these silly rules then really, have we gained as a
community?

Matt the Philosopher
